Rank every activity by how many people's output it moves, and spend your hours accordingly.

sparks.hook: A manager's output is measured in other people's work.
sparks.insight: Individual contributors are judged by what they make. Managers are judged by what their group makes, plus what other groups make because of their influence, and by nothing else. That definition is uncomfortable because it means a productive-feeling day of personal work can be worthless, while an hour that unblocks six people is enormously valuable even though you produced no artefact. It also means influence outside your reporting line counts fully: advice, standards and information that improve another team's output belong in your total.
sparks.why: Defining output at the level of the organisation makes managerial time comparable to other investments. It is the only definition under which prioritising your calendar becomes a solvable problem.
sparks.apply: Review last week's calendar and write beside each block how many people's work it changed. Cut the ones where the answer was zero.

sparks.hook: Rank your hours by how many people's work each one moves.
sparks.insight: If output is what the organisation produces, then a manager's central skill is choosing activities with high leverage: things that affect many people, that affect them over a long period, or that shift a critical decision at the moment it is still cheap to shift. Approving a plan early has enormous leverage. Reviewing the same plan after three months of work has almost none, and worse, negative leverage arrives too: a leader's visible indecision or bad mood multiplies across everyone who has to work around it.
sparks.why: Leverage explains why some managers with the same hours produce far more than others. It also explains why interruption and delay are so costly at senior levels, where the multiplier is largest.
sparks.apply: Identify one recurring decision you make late in a process and move it two weeks earlier. Measure the rework it prevents.

sparks.hook: Catch the mistake at the cheapest possible stage. It never gets cheaper.
sparks.insight: Any production process, whether it makes chips or software or contracts, has a rule: the cost of fixing a problem rises sharply at each stage the problem survives. Rejecting a faulty component before it enters the line costs almost nothing; discovering the same fault in a finished product costs a rebuild plus a customer. So the discipline is to place your inspection early, and to be willing to stop and fix rather than push a known problem forward because a deadline is close. Pushing it forward is always more expensive than it looks.
sparks.why: The cost multiplier is structural: each stage adds value that gets destroyed when the underlying fault surfaces. This is the same logic behind reviewing designs before building and testing before shipping.
sparks.apply: Add one checkpoint at the earliest stage of your team's process where a serious error could still be caught for free, and give someone authority to stop.

sparks.hook: Measure anything alone and you will get exactly that, and nothing else.
sparks.insight: Every indicator invites people to optimise it at the expense of something you did not measure. Count tickets closed and quality falls. Count lines shipped and complexity grows. The correction is to pair each measure with its natural opposite: volume with quality, speed with error rate, cost with customer satisfaction. Watching the pair together tells you something a single number cannot, and it removes the incentive to win on one dimension by quietly sacrificing another that nobody is looking at.
sparks.why: Any single measure is a partial description of the work, and the gap between the measure and the actual goal is where gaming happens. Pairing closes the most obvious gaps cheaply.
sparks.apply: For every metric on your team dashboard, add its counterweight this week. Delete any metric whose counterweight you cannot name.

sparks.hook: Meetings are not what stops managerial work. They are the work.
sparks.insight: Complaining about meetings treats them as an interruption to the real job, when for a manager they are the medium through which the job happens: information moves, decisions get made, standards get set. The useful distinction is between meetings that run continuously to keep information flowing and meetings called to reach one specific decision. The first kind should be scheduled, predictable and disciplined. The second should have a named decision, a named decider, and no attendees who are not required to make it.
sparks.why: Framing meetings as the medium rather than the obstacle changes the question from how to have fewer to how to run each type correctly, which is where the actual waste is.
sparks.apply: Label every recurring meeting in your calendar as information-flow or decision, then give the decision ones a named owner and a stated question.

carousel.title: The private conversation
carousel.body: A recurring one-to-one where the report sets the agenda. Its purpose is teaching and surfacing problems early, which is the highest-leverage use of a manager's hour.

carousel.title: The team meeting
carousel.body: Peers together with the manager, handling matters that affect several people at once. It exists so information reaches everyone in the same version at the same time.

carousel.title: The wider review
carousel.body: Groups that do not normally meet present work and get questioned. Its real function is exposure: people learn how other parts of the business think about problems.

carousel.title: The decision meeting
carousel.body: Called for one specific question, with the smallest group that can answer it. It ends with a decision recorded and an owner, or it has failed regardless of how good the discussion was.

sparks.hook: Ninety minutes with one person can shape two weeks of their work.
sparks.insight: The recurring private conversation is the highest-leverage meeting available to a manager, and it should be long enough that the other person is willing to raise something difficult. It is not a status update; the useful material is the problem they have been sitting on, the customer they are worried about, the technical decision they are unsure of. The manager's job is mostly to ask one more question than feels necessary, because the first answer is usually the prepared one and the second is the real one.
sparks.why: This is a mutual teaching session and an early warning system. Problems raised here cost an hour; the same problems discovered in a project review cost weeks.
sparks.apply: Schedule weekly one-on-ones of at least forty-five minutes, ask your report to bring the agenda, and keep asking after their first answer.

sparks.hook: Disagree fully, decide clearly, then support it as if you had won.
sparks.insight: Good organisational decisions have a shape. Everyone with real knowledge argues openly, and rank does not settle technical questions. Then a clear decision is made and stated, by a named person, with a date. Then everyone supports it in public regardless of which side they took, because an organisation cannot execute a decision that half its members are still relitigating in corridors. Skipping the first stage produces resentment and hidden resistance. Skipping the second produces drift. Skipping the third produces politics.
sparks.why: Each stage fails differently and visibly. Most organisations are chronically weak at exactly one of the three, and naming which one is usually enough to start fixing it.
sparks.apply: At the end of your next contested meeting, state the decision, the owner and the date out loud, and ask everyone to commit to it publicly.

carousel.title: Open the argument properly
carousel.body: Get the people with direct knowledge into the room and make it safe for them to contradict senior people. Silence here is not agreement, it is information you failed to collect.

carousel.title: Name the decider in advance
carousel.body: Say before the debate who will decide and by when. Ambiguity about who owns the call is what turns a technical disagreement into a political one.

carousel.title: State the decision explicitly
carousel.body: Write down what was decided, who owns it and when it takes effect. A decision everyone thinks they understood differently is not a decision, it is a delay.

carousel.title: Require visible support
carousel.body: Ask people who disagreed to back the outcome in front of their teams. Private dissent after a decision costs more than the wrong choice usually does.

sparks.hook: There is no best management style. There is only the right one for this task.
sparks.insight: How closely you should supervise someone depends not on their general seniority but on how experienced they are at the specific task in front of them. A brilliant engineer running their first negotiation needs detailed direction; the same person writing code needs none. Managers get this wrong in both directions, either micromanaging veterans or leaving a capable newcomer to fail alone at something they have never done. When someone stumbles, the first question is not whether they are good, but whether the style you applied matched the task.
sparks.why: Task-relevant experience varies within a person, not just between people. Treating style as a fixed personal trait produces both over-management and abandonment, often on the same team in the same week.
sparks.apply: For each direct report, list their current tasks and rate their experience at each one. Adjust how closely you supervise task by task, not person by person.

sparks.hook: Someone is underperforming for one of two reasons. There is no third one.
sparks.insight: When someone is not doing their job, exactly two explanations exist: they cannot do it, or they do not want to. Everything else is a symptom of one of these. That is a blunt frame and a useful one, because the two have completely different remedies and managers routinely apply the wrong one. Motivational pressure applied to a capability gap produces anxiety and no improvement. Training applied to someone who has quietly stopped caring produces an expensive course and no change either.
sparks.why: The diagnosis is easy to test: could they do it if their life depended on it? A yes points to motivation, a no points to training, and the answer determines the entire response.
sparks.apply: For your weakest performer, answer the life-depends-on-it question honestly, then choose either a training plan or a motivation conversation, not both.

sparks.hook: Training your own people is your job, not a department's.
sparks.insight: Teaching people how to do their work is among the highest-leverage things a manager can do, because a few hours of preparation improves the output of everyone in the room for years. It is also the first thing dropped when the quarter gets busy, precisely because the return arrives late and never appears on this month's numbers. Outsourcing it entirely to a training function fails for a specific reason: the person who knows what good work looks like here, and whose standards actually apply, is the manager.
sparks.why: Leverage is the ratio of hours invested to output changed, and training has one of the best ratios available. The delay in payback is what makes it feel optional and what makes it get skipped.
sparks.apply: Pick one thing your team does inconsistently and prepare a one-hour session teaching it yourself. Run it within a fortnight.

sparks.hook: Rules, contracts or culture. Which one applies depends on the situation.
sparks.insight: Organisations coordinate behaviour in three ways. Where interests are aligned and the situation is simple, prices and self-interest handle it. Where the situation is more complex but interests still roughly align, written agreements and procedures work. Where things are highly uncertain and nobody can specify in advance what should happen, only shared values keep people acting sensibly. Trying to run a fast-changing, ambiguous situation on detailed procedure is the most common and most expensive mismatch, and it usually produces more procedure.
sparks.why: The right mode depends on how uncertain the environment is and how far individual and group interests diverge. Writing more rules for an ambiguous situation adds cost without adding coordination.
sparks.apply: Identify one area where your team keeps adding process without improving outcomes, and replace the next rule with a stated principle instead.

actions: Redefine your own job description in one line as the output of your organisation plus your influence on neighbouring ones, and share it with your team.
Audit two weeks of your calendar for leverage, then delete or delegate every recurring commitment that changes nobody's work but your own.
Set up weekly one-on-ones with an agenda owned by the other person, and treat them as the first thing protected when the schedule gets tight.
Pair every metric your team reports with a counterweight measure, and remove any number that has no honest counterweight.
not_for_you_if: You want warmth and stories. This is a precise, slightly cold operating manual written by an engineer, with examples drawn from 1980s manufacturing.

verification.notes: First published 1983 by Random House, with a revised edition in 1995. Grove was chief operating officer of Intel at the time of writing. All prose original.

title: The Toyota Way
subtitle: 14 Management Principles from the World's Greatest Manufacturer
author: Jeffrey K. Liker
why_it_matters: It explained the Toyota production system as a management philosophy rather than a toolkit, which is exactly the distinction most companies copying it got wrong. It remains the clearest account of why the tools fail without the culture underneath.

crux.headline: The tools are the easy part. The culture is the system
crux.body: Anyone can install cards on a board, hold stand-up meetings and label the storage bins. What cannot be installed is an organisation that stops work to fix a small problem, promotes leaders who understand the work from having done it, and accepts a worse quarter to protect a better decade. Companies that copied the visible mechanisms without that foundation got the vocabulary and none of the results, which is the most repeated failure in modern operations.

sparks.hook: Every other principle depends on being willing to lose money this quarter.
sparks.insight: The foundation is a willingness to make decisions on a long horizon even when they damage short-term financial results. That sounds like a platitude until you see what it licenses: refusing to lay off skilled workers in a downturn because rebuilding that knowledge takes a decade, investing in suppliers who are not yet good enough, stopping production over a defect that a customer would probably never notice. None of that survives in a company that is optimised quarter by quarter, which is why the rest of the system rarely transplants.
sparks.why: Every practice downstream costs money in the short run and pays back over years. Without the willingness to absorb that gap, an organisation adopts the cheap visible parts and drops the expensive ones.
sparks.apply: Identify one decision you are making for this quarter's numbers that you would reverse on a ten-year horizon, and reverse it.

sparks.hook: Inventory is not a buffer. It is a blanket over your problems.
sparks.insight: Large stocks of unfinished work look like prudence and function as concealment. If a step is unreliable, a big pile in front of the next step means nobody notices for weeks. Shrink the pile and the unreliability becomes visible immediately and painfully, which is the entire point. Reducing batch sizes and moving toward one-piece flow is not primarily about saving storage cost; it is a deliberate way of removing the cushion so that problems surface while they are still small enough to understand.
sparks.why: Queues decouple steps and hide the variation between them. Removing the queue forces the underlying problem into view, which is uncomfortable and is the only way it gets fixed.
sparks.apply: Halve the batch size in one part of your process and watch what breaks first. Fix that rather than restoring the buffer.

sparks.hook: Build what the next step just took, not what the forecast said.
sparks.insight: A push system makes things according to a plan written in advance and hopes demand cooperates. A pull system makes something only when the step downstream has consumed the previous one, so the actual rate of consumption sets the rate of production. The difference shows up as cash: push systems accumulate stock nobody ordered, absorb capital and then need discounting to clear. Pull systems carry less, respond faster to real changes in demand, and reveal forecasting errors within days rather than at the end of a season.
sparks.why: Forecasts are wrong in proportion to how far ahead they reach. Pull replaces a long-range prediction with a short-range signal, which is a strictly better source of information.
sparks.apply: Pick one internal handoff and switch it to a pull signal: the downstream team requests work rather than the upstream team pushing it.

sparks.hook: Uneven workload does as much damage as outright waste.
sparks.insight: Most improvement programmes hunt only for obvious waste: the wasted motion, the redundant step, the idle wait. Two other problems cause at least as much harm and are usually invisible. Overburden pushes people and equipment beyond safe limits, producing errors, breakdowns and burnout. Unevenness, the peaks and troughs of a lumpy schedule, forces you to staff for the peak and pay for it in the trough. Smoothing the load often removes more waste than attacking waste directly ever will.
sparks.why: Waste, overburden and unevenness are linked: unevenness creates overburden at the peaks, and overburden generates waste through errors and rework. Levelling the schedule attacks the cause rather than the symptom.
sparks.apply: Plot the past twelve weeks of your team's incoming work. If it is lumpy, smooth the release schedule before hiring or adding tooling.

sparks.hook: Let anyone halt the whole line, and quality goes up rather than down.
sparks.insight: Giving every worker the authority to stop production over a defect sounds like a recipe for chaos and paralysis. In practice it produces the opposite, because it makes problems immediate and public rather than deferred and deniable. A stoppage costs minutes now; the same defect discovered by a customer costs a recall and a reputation. The deeper effect is cultural: when stopping is expected rather than punished, people report problems early, and the organisation gets a stream of small correctable faults instead of occasional catastrophes.
sparks.why: Quality inspected at the end can only sort good from bad. Quality built in requires the ability to stop at the moment of the fault, which requires that stopping is genuinely safe for the person doing it.
sparks.apply: Give one team explicit authority to halt a release or a shipment over a quality concern, and publicly back the first person who uses it.

sparks.hook: You cannot improve a process that is done differently every time.
sparks.insight: Standardised work is often heard as bureaucracy imposed on skilled people, and done badly that is exactly what it becomes. Done properly it is the opposite: a written best-known method that anyone doing the work can challenge and change, which then becomes the new standard. The purpose is measurement. Without a stable baseline you cannot tell whether a change helped, so improvement becomes a matter of opinion and the loudest person wins. The standard exists to be replaced, and the people doing the work own it.
sparks.why: Improvement requires a controlled comparison. A process that varies freely produces noise, and in noise every change can be defended and none can be evaluated.
sparks.apply: Write down the current best-known method for one recurring task, then let the people doing it propose the first revision within a month.

sparks.hook: Go and look yourself. A report is someone else's summary of what happened.
sparks.insight: Managers routinely decide about work they have never watched, using numbers assembled by people with a stake in how the numbers look. Going to where the work actually happens and observing it directly gives you information that no dashboard contains: the workaround everyone has adopted, the machine that is fine except on Mondays, the form nobody fills in properly because it makes no sense. This is not a symbolic visit. It means standing there long enough to see the process run several times without interrupting it.
sparks.why: Summaries lose exactly the anomalies that matter, because summarising means discarding the unusual. Direct observation is the only reliable way to recover them.
sparks.apply: Spend two hours this month watching your team's most important process run, taking notes and asking nothing until the end.

sparks.hook: Keep asking why until you reach something you can actually change.
sparks.insight: Most problem-solving stops at the first plausible cause, which is usually a person who made a mistake. Continuing to ask why moves you past the individual and into the system that made the mistake likely: the ambiguous instruction, the tool that fails silently, the schedule that guaranteed someone would be rushing. The number of questions is not sacred; what matters is continuing until you find a cause that is inside your control and whose removal would prevent recurrence rather than merely punishing this occurrence.
sparks.why: Stopping early produces blame and no fix, because the same conditions remain in place for the next person. Systemic causes are less satisfying to identify and are the only ones worth acting on.
sparks.apply: Take last month's worst error and write the chain of causes until you reach one you can change. Change it and record the date.

carousel.title: Describe what happened
carousel.body: Write the observable facts before any interpretation: what was produced, when it was noticed, what it cost. Explanations offered in the first five minutes are almost always wrong.

carousel.title: Go and see the conditions
carousel.body: Look at the actual workstation, code path or document. Reconstructing an incident from memory in a meeting room reliably produces a tidy story that never happened.

carousel.title: Ask why past the person
carousel.body: Each answer becomes the next question. The moment an answer names an individual rather than a condition, ask what made that behaviour the sensible thing to do.

carousel.title: Change one condition
carousel.body: Pick a cause inside your control and alter it, then check weeks later whether the problem recurred. A countermeasure that is never verified is just a meeting outcome.

sparks.hook: Decide slowly with everyone, then implement faster than anyone.
sparks.insight: Spending weeks circulating a proposal, gathering objections and revising it before any formal decision looks painfully slow to organisations that prize decisiveness. The trade is deliberate. By the time the decision is made, every objection has been heard, every affected group has contributed, and implementation meets almost no resistance. The alternative, a fast decision followed by months of quiet obstruction and rework, is usually slower end to end while feeling more dynamic on the day it is announced.
sparks.why: Total elapsed time includes implementation, not just the decision. Front-loading disagreement moves the friction to the cheapest point, before anyone has built anything.
sparks.apply: Before your next significant decision, circulate the proposal to everyone affected and require each to submit one objection in writing.

sparks.hook: Grow your leaders inside, or import someone who will change the answer.
sparks.insight: Organisations under pressure hire senior leaders from outside for their track record, and often get a competent person who does not understand what made this particular place work. A system built on deep knowledge of the actual work requires leaders who have done that work and absorbed the philosophy over years, which means promoting from within is a structural requirement rather than a sentimental preference. The cost is real: internal development is slow, and the pipeline has to be built long before you need it.
sparks.why: Where advantage lives in accumulated practice rather than in strategy documents, an outsider cannot bring it and can unintentionally dismantle it while making sensible-looking changes.
sparks.apply: Name your successor and the two people behind them, then give each a stretch assignment this year that develops the gap you identified.

sparks.hook: Respect means giving people hard problems, not making them comfortable.
sparks.insight: Respect for people is easily misread as a pleasant workplace with good benefits. What it means here is harder and more flattering: assume the people doing the work are the ones who understand it, give them genuinely difficult problems, teach them the method, and then expect them to solve things rather than escalate them. The same logic extends outward to suppliers, who get demanding targets, long relationships and real technical help rather than an annual auction on price.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: the record is not spotless. Toyota's large safety recalls around 2009 and 2010 raised serious questions about whether rapid global growth had outrun the system, and many Western lean programmes have copied the tools while producing none of the results.
sparks.apply: Give one team a problem you would normally solve for them, plus the method and a deadline, and resist providing the answer.

carousel.title: Start with the philosophy
carousel.body: Agree what the organisation is for on a ten-year view. Every later practice costs money in the short run, so without this the programme is cancelled at the first bad quarter.

carousel.title: Fix the process next
carousel.body: Create flow, level the load and make problems visible. This is the layer most companies buy consultants for and the only one they usually implement.

carousel.title: Develop people and partners
carousel.body: Grow leaders internally, teach the method rather than the tools, and treat suppliers as long-term participants who deserve help rather than annual price pressure.

carousel.title: Make problem-solving continuous
carousel.body: Go and see, ask why past the person, reflect honestly on what went wrong, and keep improving in small increments forever rather than in occasional programmes.

actions: Pick one process and cut its batch size or queue in half, then fix the first problem that surfaces instead of restoring the buffer.
Spend two hours observing your most important process directly, writing down every workaround people have quietly invented to make it work.
Run a proper root-cause session on your worst recent failure, continuing past the first person named until you reach a condition you can change.
Name the long-term decision your current quarterly targets are pushing you to get wrong, and take it to your leadership team with the ten-year case.
not_for_you_if: You work in a small service business with no repeatable process, or you want a short toolkit rather than a long account of manufacturing culture.

verification.notes: Published 2004 by McGraw-Hill. Liker is a professor of industrial engineering who has studied Toyota since the 1980s. A second edition appeared in 2021. All prose original.

title: Reengineering the Corporation
subtitle: A Manifesto for Business Revolution
author: Michael Hammer and James Champy
why_it_matters: It moved the unit of analysis in management from the department to the end-to-end process, which is now so standard that it is invisible. It also became the decade's most abused idea, and both halves of that story are worth knowing.

crux.headline: Redesign the work, do not speed up the mess
crux.body: Most business processes were not designed at all. They accreted, one department at a time, until a simple request touched nine functions and spent most of its life waiting in trays. Automating that shape makes a bad process faster and more permanent. The alternative is to start from what the customer actually needs, ask why each step exists, and rebuild the flow around the whole outcome rather than around the boundaries of your organisation chart.

sparks.hook: Automating a broken process gives you a broken process at higher speed.
sparks.insight: The instinct when work is slow is to buy software for it. That preserves every handoff, approval and duplicate record, encodes them in a system that is now expensive to change, and delivers a modest improvement that everyone celebrates. The alternative question is more uncomfortable: if we were designing this from nothing, knowing what customers need and what technology can do, would any of these steps exist? Usually a third of them would not, and the technology decision looks completely different once that is settled.
sparks.why: Technology applied to an unexamined process locks in its assumptions. The cost of change afterwards rises sharply, which is why so many organisations are still running the shape of a 1990s workflow.
sparks.apply: Before your next system purchase, map the process it will automate and delete every step that exists only because of an old organisational boundary.

sparks.hook: Most of the time in your process is waiting, not working.
sparks.insight: Measure a request from arrival to completion and then measure the time anyone actually spends on it. In most organisations the working time is a tiny fraction of the elapsed time, and everything else is queueing between departments. That means effort spent making individual steps faster is aimed at the small part of the problem. The large part is the number of handoffs, and each handoff adds a queue, a chance to lose context, a chance to introduce an error, and a person who can now blame someone else.
sparks.why: Handoffs are where both delay and defects concentrate, because responsibility becomes ambiguous exactly at the boundary. Reducing their number attacks both problems at once.
sparks.apply: Time one real request end to end, then count the working minutes inside it. Present the ratio to your team and count the handoffs.

carousel.title: Pick one real case
carousel.body: Take a single actual request rather than an average or a description of how the process is supposed to run. Averages hide the waiting, which is the thing you are looking for.

carousel.title: Follow it, do not model it
carousel.body: Track where it physically sits each day and who is holding it. Most of the surprises come from queues nobody counts because the work is technically assigned to someone.

carousel.title: Count working minutes
carousel.body: Add up the time anyone actually touched it and divide by the elapsed time. The number is usually small enough to end the argument about which step to optimise.

carousel.title: Count the handoffs
carousel.body: Every transfer between people or teams is a queue plus a chance to lose context. Reducing that count moves the ratio far more than making any single step faster.

sparks.hook: Give one person the whole job and the queues disappear with the handoffs.
sparks.insight: Splitting work into narrow specialised tasks was a genuine advance when coordination was expensive and workers could not see the whole picture. Modern information systems remove that constraint: one person, or one small team, can now own a request from beginning to end because they can see everything and reach everyone. The gains are not only speed. A single owner can answer a customer's question without transferring the call, spot problems that only appear across the whole flow, and cannot pass responsibility sideways.
sparks.why: Specialisation optimises each step and ignores the connections. When most of the cost lives in the connections, consolidating ownership wins even if each individual step becomes slightly less efficient.
sparks.apply: Pick one process with more than four handoffs and give a single named owner responsibility for the whole thing for a trial quarter.

sparks.hook: Let the people who need the output do the work themselves.
sparks.insight: Departments exist partly because a task once required scarce expertise or equipment. When that stops being true, the department remains and everyone routes requests through it, adding a queue for something the requester could now do directly. Purchasing small items, running a standard report, provisioning an environment: each was once specialist work and is now a form and a wait. The redesign is to push the work to whoever wants the result, with guardrails, and keep the specialists for the cases that genuinely need them.
sparks.why: The department's original justification is rarely re-examined after the constraint disappears. Its continued existence then generates real cost in waiting time across everyone else's work.
sparks.apply: Find one internal request queue where the requester could safely do the task themselves, and give them the access plus a simple limit.

sparks.hook: Most approvals cost more than the losses they prevent.
sparks.insight: Controls accumulate one incident at a time. Something goes wrong, an approval step is added, and nobody ever removes it. Eventually a process contains layers of checking whose combined cost, counting delay and management time as well as salary, far exceeds the value of the errors they catch. The honest test is arithmetic rather than principle: what does this control cost per year, and what would the losses be without it? Where the second number is smaller, the sensible design is to accept the losses and check afterwards.
sparks.why: Controls are added in response to vivid single events and removed almost never, so the stock only grows. Aggregate control cost is invisible because it is spread across everyone's waiting time.
sparks.apply: Pick your most annoying approval step, estimate its annual cost in delay, and compare it with the losses it has actually prevented.

sparks.hook: One process built for the worst case punishes every simple case.
sparks.insight: Organisations design a single procedure that can handle the most complex, highest-risk version of a request, then force every routine case through it. The result is that ninety percent of the work carries the overhead of the ten percent. A better design is several versions with a quick sort at the front: a simple path for straightforward cases, a full path for complicated ones, and a clear rule for which is which. This used to be impractical because sorting was expensive, and it no longer is.
sparks.why: Averaging a process across a varied caseload optimises for none of it. Multiple paths are only workable when the triage rule is explicit and cheap, which modern systems make possible.
sparks.apply: Split one process into a fast lane and a full lane, defining in writing which cases qualify for the fast lane and who decides.

sparks.hook: Every department can hit its targets while the customer waits three weeks.
sparks.insight: Functional measurement is the quiet reason process redesign fails. Each department is judged on its own efficiency, so each optimises its own step, batches work to reduce its unit cost, and pushes queues onto its neighbours. Everyone reports success and the end-to-end time gets worse. Unless someone measures the whole flow from the customer's request to the customer's outcome, and holds a single person accountable for that number, local incentives will slowly rebuild every handoff you removed.
sparks.why: Measurement determines behaviour more reliably than redesign does. A process rebuilt without changing the metrics reverts, usually within a year and without anyone deciding to reverse it.
sparks.apply: Publish one end-to-end cycle time from the customer's point of view every week, and give a single named person accountability for it.

sparks.hook: Redesigning a process means starting from the outcome, not the org chart.
sparks.insight: The method is uncomfortable because it forbids the natural starting point. You do not begin with the current process and improve it; you begin with what the customer needs and design backwards, treating existing departments, systems and job titles as things to be justified rather than assumed. Most of the effort goes into resisting the pull back toward the familiar shape, which is why these efforts nearly always require someone senior enough to overrule the people whose territory is being redrawn.
sparks.why: Improvement from the current state converges on a local optimum shaped by history. Starting from the outcome is the only way to reach a different shape, and it is politically expensive by design.
sparks.apply: Take your slowest customer-facing process and sketch how you would build it from scratch today, with no reference to who currently owns each step.

carousel.title: Choose the right process
carousel.body: Pick one that is genuinely broken, genuinely matters to customers, and is realistically changeable. Getting any of those three wrong wastes a year of political capital.

carousel.title: Understand it, do not document it
carousel.body: Learn what customers actually need and where time goes. Producing an exhaustive map of the current mess is a common substitute for changing it.

carousel.title: Design from the outcome backwards
carousel.body: Start with the result and add only steps that earn their place. Existing departments and systems are constraints to be argued with, not the frame for the design.

carousel.title: Change the measures with it
carousel.body: Move accountability to one owner of the whole flow and report end-to-end time. Without this the old functional incentives quietly rebuild the process you removed.

sparks.hook: This cannot be delegated. It crosses exactly the lines you drew.
sparks.insight: Process redesign fails when it is handed to a middle manager or a consulting team, because a real process crosses several departments and every one of them has a leader with budget, headcount and a strong view about their own boundary. Nobody below the level where those departments meet can make the trade-off, so the effort produces a recommendation that gets negotiated into a small improvement inside one function. The sponsor has to be senior enough to lose a department a headcount and mean it.
sparks.why: Authority has to match the scope of the change. Cross-functional redesign attempted without cross-functional authority reliably degrades into a departmental efficiency project.
sparks.apply: Before starting any process redesign, confirm which single executive can move budget and headcount between the affected departments. If none can, do not start.

sparks.hook: The idea was sound. What companies did with it mostly was not.
sparks.insight: Through the 1990s the label became cover for headcount reduction. Firms announced a redesign, cut staff, changed little about how work actually flowed, and left the survivors doing the same broken process with fewer people. The word acquired a permanent association with layoffs that it has never lost. Hammer himself later acknowledged that the original argument gave too little weight to the people doing the work, and a great many programmes delivered nothing close to what was promised.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: this is a genuinely important idea with a bad record in practice. The core insight about end-to-end process survives; the promise of dramatic transformation on a fixed timetable does not.
sparks.apply: If you use this method, state up front what happens to the people whose roles change, and publish that alongside the redesign.

actions: Time one real customer request end to end and calculate what fraction of the elapsed time is actual work. Share the ratio with the departments involved.
Pick one process with many handoffs, appoint a single owner for the whole flow, and publish an end-to-end cycle time they are accountable for.
Audit the approval steps in one process, estimate the annual cost of each in delay, and remove any whose cost exceeds the losses it prevents.
Split a high-volume process into a fast lane and a full lane with a written rule for which cases go where, then measure both for a quarter.
not_for_you_if: You want a balanced treatment. This is written as a manifesto, its confidence outran its evidence, and the surrounding history matters as much as the method.

verification.notes: Published 1993 by HarperBusiness. Hammer died in 2008. Champy published a follow-up on management in 1995, and a revised edition of this book appeared in 2003. All prose original.

title: Competing Against Luck
subtitle: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
author: Clayton M. Christensen
why_it_matters: It gives product teams a unit of analysis that is neither the customer nor the product but the progress someone is trying to make. That reframing does more to explain purchase behaviour than any amount of demographic segmentation.

crux.headline: Nobody wants your product. They want progress
crux.body: People do not buy things because of who they are. They buy because something happened in their life that they need to make better, and your product was the least bad option available at that moment. Understand the circumstance, the struggle, and what the alternatives were, and the design questions answer themselves. Understand only the customer's age, income and category preferences and you will keep building features that correlate with buyers and cause nothing.

sparks.hook: People do not buy products. They hire them for a job and fire them later.
sparks.insight: Think of every purchase as a hiring decision. Something happened, a person had a problem, they looked at the options available and hired one to get the job done. If it does the job they hire it again; if something better shows up they fire it without sentiment. The useful shift is that the job stays stable for decades while products and technologies churn. Design for the job and you have a durable target. Design for the current product category and you are aiming at something that will be gone in ten years.
sparks.why: Jobs describe a stable need in a specific circumstance, which is why they predict behaviour better than product attributes or customer characteristics do.
sparks.apply: Interview five recent customers about the day they decided to buy, and write the job as a sentence starting with the situation, not the person.

sparks.hook: The same product is two different products at eight in the morning.
sparks.insight: A well-known consulting study of milkshake sales found that a large share were bought early by solo drivers, who wanted something thick enough to last a boring commute and manageable with one hand. The afternoon buyers were parents saying yes to a child, and they wanted something small and quick. Same product, same shop, two entirely different jobs, with opposite improvement paths. Averaging the two customers produces a milkshake that fails both, which is what conventional market research would have recommended.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: this is a consulting anecdote from fieldwork, not a controlled study, and it is retold far more often than it is tested. Its value is as a demonstration of the method, not as evidence.
sparks.apply: Segment your usage data by time and situation rather than by customer type, and look for two groups doing genuinely different things.

sparks.hook: Your real competitor might be a spreadsheet, or doing nothing at all.
sparks.insight: Companies define competition by category, so a software firm watches other software firms. Customers define it by the job, so the actual alternatives include a manual workaround, a colleague who does it as a favour, a completely different kind of product, and most often the option of continuing to put up with the problem. That last one wins more competitive battles than any rival, and it is invisible in any analysis that only studies people who already bought something in your category.
sparks.why: Defining your competitive set by the job rather than the category reveals substitutes you were not tracking, and explains lost deals that appear to have been lost to nobody.
sparks.apply: Ask ten prospects who did not buy what they are doing instead. Count how many chose a workaround or nothing at all.

sparks.hook: Knowing who buys tells you nothing about why they bought.
sparks.insight: Customer data gets richer every year and mostly describes correlations: this group buys more, that segment churns faster, users who do this action retain better. None of it explains the mechanism, and building product from correlation produces features aimed at a pattern rather than a cause. The alternative is slower and less scalable: talk to people about a specific purchase, reconstruct what happened in the days around it, and find out what they were trying to accomplish. That is where causal information lives.
sparks.why: Correlation supports targeting and prediction but not design, because it cannot tell you which attribute did the work. Only reconstructing the decision gives you something to build on.
sparks.apply: Replace one segmentation study with ten switching interviews this quarter and compare which produces a decision you actually change.

sparks.hook: Find the moment they got fed up. That is where the demand lives.
sparks.insight: Purchases are triggered by a specific moment when the current arrangement stopped being tolerable: something broke, a deadline appeared, a routine changed, an embarrassment happened. Interviewing for that moment produces very different information than asking what people want, because people are poor at describing their preferences and quite good at recounting what happened. The interview is closer to reconstructing an incident than to a survey, and the most valuable material comes from what they tried first and why it did not work.
sparks.why: Recall of a specific event is far more reliable than stated preference, and the sequence of failed attempts tells you exactly what the alternatives were and where they fell short.
sparks.apply: Find three customers who switched recently and walk them through the week before, hour by hour, without mentioning your product.

carousel.title: Find recent switchers
carousel.body: Talk to people who changed something in the past few weeks. Memory of the decision decays fast, and anyone who bought a year ago will reconstruct a tidy rational story.

carousel.title: Rebuild the timeline backwards
carousel.body: Start from the purchase and work back to the first moment they thought about it. You are looking for the trigger event, which is usually earlier and smaller than expected.

carousel.title: Ask what they tried first
carousel.body: Almost nobody buys as a first move. The failed workarounds tell you what the job really is and which alternatives you are actually competing with.

carousel.title: Listen for anxiety and habit
carousel.body: Ask what nearly stopped them buying and what they had to give up. These forces explain your stalled pipeline better than any feature comparison will.

sparks.hook: The functional job gets you shortlisted. The emotional one closes the sale.
sparks.insight: Every job has a practical dimension, which is what a spec sheet captures, and it also has social and emotional dimensions that usually decide the outcome. Someone choosing a service is often buying the ability to stop worrying, to look competent in front of their boss, or to avoid a conversation they dread. Those are rarely mentioned unprompted and almost never appear in requirements documents, yet they explain why the technically superior option loses and why price sensitivity vanishes when the anxiety is genuinely removed.
sparks.why: People report functional reasons because they are socially acceptable. The emotional and social dimensions surface only when you ask about a specific event rather than about criteria.
sparks.apply: For your main product, write the functional, social and emotional part of the job separately, then check which one your marketing actually addresses.

sparks.hook: Four forces decide every switch, and two of them are working against you.
sparks.insight: Any change of behaviour is a contest between four pressures. The current situation has to be annoying enough to push someone out of it, and the new option has to be attractive enough to pull them in. Working against both are anxiety about the new thing going wrong, and the ordinary gravity of an existing habit that mostly works. Product teams pour almost all their effort into the pull and almost none into reducing anxiety or breaking habit, which is why so many demonstrably better products fail to be adopted.
sparks.why: The two opposing forces are usually larger than the difference in product quality, and they are cheaper to address. Refunds, migration help and trials attack anxiety directly.
sparks.apply: List the three things a prospective customer is worried about, then remove or guarantee each one before adding another feature.

carousel.title: The push of the situation
carousel.body: Something has to be wrong enough to make the person look for an alternative. If nothing is pushing them, no amount of product quality starts the process.

carousel.title: The pull of the new option
carousel.body: Your product has to offer a visible, believable improvement on that specific struggle. Generic superiority is not a pull; it is a claim nobody has time to evaluate.

carousel.title: Anxiety about switching
carousel.body: Fear of losing data, wasting money, or looking foolish in front of colleagues. Guarantees, trials and migration help remove more friction than most feature work.

carousel.title: The habit of the present
carousel.body: The current arrangement is known and mostly works. Beating it requires making the first week of the new thing easier than the hundredth week of the old one.

sparks.hook: The people who buy nothing are the biggest market in most categories.
sparks.insight: Analysis of a market usually counts existing customers of existing products, which excludes everyone who has a real struggle and rejected every current option as too expensive, too complicated or not worth the trouble. That group is frequently much larger than the served market and is invisible to conventional research, because they have no purchase history. They are also the easiest group to serve, since the standard they compare against is doing nothing rather than a well-funded competitor's polished product.
sparks.why: Market sizing based on current sales measures what has already been sold, not what people need. The gap between the two is where most genuinely new categories come from.
sparks.apply: Identify people with the job you serve who currently buy nothing, and ask what would need to be true for the cheapest possible version to be worth it.

sparks.hook: The job is done by the whole experience, not by the feature.
sparks.insight: A customer does not hire a feature; they hire everything that happens from the moment they decide to the moment the struggle is resolved. That includes buying, setting up, learning, getting help when it breaks and eventually leaving. A product that is excellent in use and painful to install fails the job as surely as one that does not work. Competitors can copy a feature quickly and find it far harder to copy an experience assembled from dozens of coordinated decisions across several departments.
sparks.why: Integrating the whole experience requires cross-functional coordination, which is expensive and slow, and that difficulty is precisely why it is defensible once built.
sparks.apply: Map every step from a customer's first search to their first success, and fix the step where the most people currently give up.

sparks.hook: As companies grow, they stop knowing customers and start knowing spreadsheets.
sparks.insight: Early on, a company knows its customers personally because there are few of them and the founders talk to them. As it scales, that knowledge is replaced by operational data about the business itself: efficiency, margin, funnel conversion. The data is easier to collect, arrives faster and is what management reviews reward, so it steadily displaces the messy qualitative understanding of why anyone buys. The organisation ends up optimising itself with great precision while gradually losing track of the job it was hired to do.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: the jobs framework is hard to falsify, and Christensen's broader disruption theory has drawn serious academic criticism, including a prominent 2014 critique in The New Yorker. Treat this as an interviewing discipline rather than a predictive law.
sparks.apply: Put a standing item in your monthly leadership meeting where someone presents one recent customer story in full, before any metrics are shown.

actions: Run ten switching interviews with people who bought or left in the past month, reconstructing the timeline of their decision rather than asking what they want.
Write your customers' job as a single sentence describing a situation and a struggle, then check whether your roadmap addresses it or addresses your category.
List the anxieties and habits keeping prospects from switching, and ship one change that removes an anxiety instead of adding a feature.
Identify the people with your job who currently buy nothing, and size that group honestly against your existing addressable market.
not_for_you_if: You want rigorous evidence. The argument is built from case studies and consulting fieldwork, and it is easier to apply after the fact than before.

verification.notes: Published 2016 by HarperBusiness, co-authored with Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon and David S. Duncan. Christensen died in 2020. All prose original.

title: Scaling Up
subtitle: How a Few Companies Make It...and Why the Rest Don't
author: Verne Harnish
why_it_matters: It is less a theory than an operating system for a company between roughly ten and a few hundred people, assembled from practices that work. For the specific problem of a business outgrowing its founders' memory, nothing else is as complete.

crux.headline: Four things break when you grow. Fix them in order
crux.body: Growth exposes the same four weaknesses in every company. You have the wrong people or the right people in unclear roles. Your strategy is not specific enough for anyone to act on without asking. Execution leaks because nobody knows this week's priority. And cash runs out faster than profit suggests, because growth consumes it. Almost every crisis in a scaling business is one of these four wearing a costume.

sparks.hook: Growth does not create new problems. It enlarges the ones you ignored.
sparks.insight: A company of eight people runs on the founders remembering everything and talking constantly. At forty that stops working, and the failure shows up as symptoms: missed handoffs, duplicated work, a good hire who quits after six months, an unexpected cash squeeze in a great quarter. The symptoms differ, the causes almost never do. They resolve into people, strategy, execution and cash, and diagnosing which one you are actually facing is more useful than treating whichever symptom is loudest this week.
sparks.why: The four categories map onto what informal coordination used to handle for free. Growth removes that subsidy, and everything it was quietly covering surfaces at roughly the same time.
sparks.apply: Take your three most annoying current problems and assign each to people, strategy, execution or cash. Fix the category with two entries in it.

sparks.hook: Profitable companies go bust. Growth is what eats the cash.
sparks.insight: Every new customer is paid for before they pay you: the stock, the salaries, the onboarding, the sales cost. So the faster you grow, the larger the gap between money going out and money coming back, and a business can be genuinely profitable on paper while running out of money in the bank. The lever most founders never pull is the length of that cycle. Shortening it by getting paid faster, holding less stock or shipping sooner funds growth from inside the business rather than from a lender.
sparks.why: Cash consumed by growth scales with the growth rate and the length of the cash cycle. That makes cycle length a lever with the same effect as raising money and no dilution.
sparks.apply: Calculate how many days pass between spending a pound and getting it back, then cut that number by ten days this quarter.

carousel.title: Shorten the sales cycle
carousel.body: Time from first contact to a signed order. Every week here is a week of salary spent before any money arrives, and it is usually the least examined part of the cycle.

carousel.title: Speed up delivery
carousel.body: Time from order to the thing being delivered or the work being done. Anything sitting half-finished is cash converted into something you cannot yet invoice for.

carousel.title: Hold less in stock
carousel.body: Materials and finished goods sitting still are money doing nothing. Smaller, more frequent replenishment usually beats bulk discounts once the cash cost is counted.

carousel.title: Bill and collect faster
carousel.body: Invoice the day you deliver, chase before the due date, and take deposits. Most companies have weeks of free funding available here and never go looking for it.

sparks.hook: If you would not enthusiastically rehire someone, you already know.
sparks.insight: The single most useful question about a team is whether, knowing everything you now know, you would hire each person again with enthusiasm. Hesitation is the answer. Most leaders already know who does not belong and spend a year building the case, during which the strongest people watch and quietly conclude that standards are negotiable. The cost of the delay is not the underperformer's salary; it is the message sent to everyone who is performing and wondering whether excellence is actually noticed.
sparks.why: Tolerating a known mismatch is read by the rest of the team as the real standard. That signal costs more than the individual does, and it compounds through every subsequent hiring decision.
sparks.apply: Score each team member on whether you would rehire them enthusiastically. For every no, act within thirty days, by coaching, moving or exiting.

sparks.hook: Two names against a job means nobody owns it.
sparks.insight: As companies grow, responsibilities blur: two people are half-responsible for pricing, three share the customer relationship, and nobody owns onboarding. Everyone believes it is handled. The correction is a chart of functions rather than people, with exactly one name and one number beside each function. It is uncomfortable to produce, because it makes visible which functions have nobody, which have several, and where a founder is still holding four jobs they should have handed over two years ago.
sparks.why: Shared accountability behaves like no accountability under pressure, because each holder can reasonably assume the other is acting. A single name plus a single measure removes the ambiguity.
sparks.apply: List every function your business needs, put one name and one number beside each, and resolve every blank or duplicate this month.

sparks.hook: The rhythm of meetings is the management system. Everything else is memory.
sparks.insight: Small companies coordinate by talking constantly. That breaks somewhere around twenty people, and the replacement is not more meetings but a fixed cadence with different purposes at each level. Short daily contact for blockers, a weekly session for one substantial issue, a monthly for learning, a quarterly for priorities, an annual for direction. The value comes from the predictability: when everyone knows the next decision point is three days away, issues stop escalating into emergencies and stop being raised in corridors.
sparks.why: A reliable cadence reduces the cost of not deciding immediately. Without it, urgency becomes the only routing mechanism and the loudest problem always wins.
sparks.apply: Install a fifteen-minute daily huddle and a ninety-minute weekly meeting with one substantive topic, and hold both for a full quarter before judging.

carousel.title: Daily, fifteen minutes
carousel.body: Standing, same time, three things each: what is happening today, the number that matters, and what is stuck. No problem solving, only routing to the right conversation.

carousel.title: Weekly, ninety minutes
carousel.body: One important issue discussed properly, plus a look at the quarterly priorities and customer feedback. This is where the real thinking happens, not in the daily.

carousel.title: Monthly, half a day
carousel.body: Managers together, reviewing progress and learning something. Its function is developing the management layer, which is the constraint on growth more often than the market is.

carousel.title: Quarterly and annual
carousel.body: Set a small number of priorities, one number that matters most, and review whether the strategy still holds. Off-site, with enough time to change your mind.

sparks.hook: If it does not fit on one page, nobody will remember it in March.
sparks.insight: Long strategic plans are read once and filed. A plan that fits on a single page, showing values, longer-term ambition, this year's targets, this quarter's priorities and who owns what, gets used because it can be held in mind and put on a wall. The constraint is the point: forcing everything onto one page requires deciding what is actually essential, and most of what gets cut turns out to have been there for reassurance rather than for direction.
sparks.why: A plan only changes behaviour if people recall it while making decisions. Length is inversely related to recall, which makes brevity a functional requirement rather than a stylistic preference.
sparks.apply: Compress your current plan onto one page with the quarterly priorities and owners visible, then put it where the team sees it daily.

sparks.hook: Five priorities with one on top, or you have not prioritised.
sparks.insight: A quarter with twelve priorities produces twelve half-finished things and a team that quietly picks its own order. The discipline is to name a small number for the quarter and then, harder still, to name which single one matters most, so that when two of them conflict in week seven everyone already knows how to resolve it without a meeting. Attaching one measurable number to that top priority makes it visible whether progress is real, which is exactly why teams resist doing it.
sparks.why: Priorities exist to settle conflicts in advance. A list without a ranking pushes the trade-off down to individuals, who resolve it inconsistently and privately.
sparks.apply: Pick five priorities for the quarter, mark one as the top, attach a number to it, and report that number every week.

sparks.hook: Values you have never fired anyone over are decoration.
sparks.insight: Most stated values are unobjectionable and therefore useless: integrity, teamwork, excellence. A value only does work if it is specific enough to rule something out and is actually used when a decision is expensive. The test is whether it has ever cost you money: a hire rejected despite being talented, a customer let go, a promotion refused to a high performer who treated colleagues badly. If no such example exists in the past two years, the values are a poster rather than a management tool.
sparks.why: Values function as pre-agreed tie-breakers for decisions where the profitable answer and the right answer diverge. A value that has never been costly has never been tested.
sparks.apply: For each stated value, find a real decision in the past year where it changed the outcome. Delete any value with no example.

sparks.hook: Promise a small number of specific things and keep them better than anyone.
sparks.insight: Broad positioning gives customers nothing to hold you to and gives your team nothing to organise around. A better approach is a handful of concrete promises that are measurable and demanding enough that competitors will not match them: a response time, a guarantee, a delivery window, a scope of support. They then become internal operating targets rather than marketing copy, and the whole company can be arranged around keeping them. The discomfort of committing publicly is what makes them useful.
sparks.why: A measurable promise couples the outside story to the inside operation. Vague positioning stays in marketing and never reaches the people whose daily decisions determine whether it is true.
sparks.apply: Write three specific promises your customers could hold you to, publish them, and put a weekly measure against each one.

sparks.hook: The job that got you to twenty people is the wrong job at eighty.
sparks.insight: Every rough tripling of headcount changes what the leader should personally do. Early on the founder does the work; then they manage the people doing it; then they build the managers; then they mostly set direction, allocate capital and appoint people. The transitions are uncomfortable because each one means giving up something you are good at and visibly enjoy, and most founders make the change a year later than they should, usually after something breaks that they were still holding onto.
sparks.why: Honest caveat: this is a practitioner's system assembled from other people's frameworks, and its evidence is case studies of client companies. In a team under ten the full meeting cadence is overhead rather than structure.
sparks.apply: List everything only you can do and everything you simply prefer doing. Hand over one item from the second list before the end of the month.

actions: Diagnose your current problems against people, strategy, execution and cash, then work on the category holding the most of them rather than the loudest symptom.
Calculate your cash conversion cycle in days and set a target to shorten it by ten days this quarter, naming an owner for each stage.
Build a one-page function chart with a single name and a single number against every function your business needs, and resolve all blanks and duplicates.
Install a daily huddle and a weekly management meeting, and run both for a full quarter before deciding whether the rhythm is working.
not_for_you_if: You run a team of fewer than ten people, or you dislike prescriptive systems assembled from other authors' frameworks and consultant case studies.

verification.notes: Published 2014 by Gazelles Inc., presented as a successor to Harnish's earlier Mastering the Rockefeller Habits. It draws openly on work by Jim Collins, Brad Smart and others. All prose original.
